## Landing ##

### Airplane ###
I woke up with an oxygen mask dangling in front of my face and a whole plane full of very confused people.

"Oh, bloody hell," I heard from the seat beside me.
"Bloody hell indeed," I replied.
A portion of the planes cabin was now on their feet, wandering, and bumping about the aisles between us, and a small portion still had their oxygen masks on. There was nothing to really worry about, but the air of panic was undeniable.
"Miss," someone called from a few rows ahead, "there's nothing to worry about... it's just air pressure, I---"
Someone passed between us and blocked the rest of the sentence, but I could guess where it was going.
I can't blame her, really, flying is scary enough, and that isn't even considering the gigantic metal tube we are all stuck inside of. I took the opportunity the commotion afforded me to get to the washroom before anyone else was comfortable enough to form a line.
I did my business, washed my hands and splashed my face a few times in anemic attempt to catch my own thoughts. With as much noise and commotion as this turbulence had caused, it made holding my head on straight	 more of a feat than usual.

*pscht*
"---Please make sure your seat backs and tray tables are in their upright positions, your seatbelts are securely fastened, and all carry-on items are stowed either under the seat in front of you or in the overhead bins.---"
*pscht*

I hobbled back to my seat, hip-checking a few men in sweatpants along the way, and shoved my laptop and whatever books I had crammed into the seat-back pocket into my Gran's bag. Feeling a pang of nerves, I rummaged through its depths for Gran's emergency snack pouch---half a bag of dried mango---and popped a piece into my mouth. With one headphone hanging loose, I spent the next half hour trying to pin it in place---the leather folds leaving an embarrassingly stubborn imprint on my forehead.

### Birmingham ###
Welcome to Birmingham read the cartoon pirate, it's print stretched along one-too-many terminal. It was busy, but that was to be expected, but it was too early for any of us to feel much in a hurry; we were just in the mood to meander to and fro, and to and fro we meandered.

"Right, yes, of course," I uttered, shaking myself out of whatever fog was sitting in and waved my ticket at the Express Lane terminal.
I have an iffy relationship with airports (if you can even call it that), I visit them often enough that I cannot help but have an impression on a few of them. They each have their eccentricities, but each existed in a world of their own: half in, half out; half homely enough to fit the city, half uncomfortable enough to keep the homeless from making the foyers their home.
This didn't always work, but it's why every airport felt as bleached and grey as every other airport. Some had their distinctive qualities, like the apocalyptic paintings in Denver, the wooden totems at Vancouver, or the wave pool at Munich, but I'm positive those exist mostly to remind people they took the right transfer.
Whether you get a Durian McFlurry in Singapore, Camembert donuts in Germany, or the McPatatas in Mexico, you are still eating at a McDonald's.

I felt a tap on my shoulder.
"Pardon?" I asked, turning around to see it was the guy from the seat beside me, he had dark skin, a fresh haircut, and new shoes, and was also waiting for his luggage.
"Did they ever give us our breakfast?"
"Goddamnit, I don't think they did," I replied, then recognizing what that feeling in the bottom of my stomach was.
We continued to exist within each others periphery as we waited until our luggage came by. It was no less awkward than one would expect.
"Where you coming here from?"
"Toronto, yourself?" When you are waiting for your luggage, everything looks like your luggage.
"Same," he said, yawning a bit of a yawn and trying to get whatever his coffee mug had left in it.
His eyebrows perked up when a blue, 100 litre spinner bag came by; mine perked when a much smaller, hard case one did. He offered to grab mine, too, and I was too tired to bother saying no.
"You come here often?" He asked.
"Not especially," I answered, "not lately."
"Mind if I offer to get you breakfast? My bosses treat...," he scratched an itch on the side of his head, "don't like to eat alone. And we can bond over a shared traumatic experience."
"Yeah," I yawned, pushed my glasses up the ridge of my nose and yawned again. Of course I could afford breakfast, I could probably even get reimbursed by Lufthansa, too, but a free meal is a free meal, and I still had to figure out what the rest of my day was going to look like.
"Yeah, sure," I repeated, not entirely sure if my previous answer had made it past my yawn.

There are three types of people at the airport --- those that have to budget their airplane trips, those that do not, and those that spend their time in the secret VIP airport lounges that none of us were supposed to know about.. The former of the three do not use luggage with wheels, and the latter of the three do not have to bother.
Well, and the kind that still has a four hour drive to make down to the other end of England.

"Bottega?" he asked.
"Yeah, sure, sounds good," he lead me past a Duty Free, a watch store, and a WHSmith bookstore on the departure lounge map I had saved on my phone. I was sitting at a solid 87% battery life and I felt like the Queen of bloody England.
We found seats right away and ordered two coffees and two waters right away, so at least I knew this guy and I were on the same wavelength.
"You come here often, then?" I asked, using my finely tuned womanly skills to figure out if he comes here often, noticing the price of the DOC Brut.
"Enough for them to notice me," he answered, "but not enough to remember where." He laughed, I laughed back.
"So," I asked with half of my laugh still on my face, "what do I call you, other than Isle Seat, I mean."
He laughed again.
"I've been called Rajesh my entire life, so we can go with that. It's a name my parents brought here from {==Puducherry==}{>>Where M. Nights family is from<<}, a small city in India."
"Well, my name is Madeleine, but I've been called Maddy my entire life."
I whipped open my menu with one hand and portioned some cream and sugar to my coffee with the other. It felt nice to speak words that were more than 'yes' or 'no,' and at more a rate than an intermittent one.

By the time the waitstaff had arrived, I had already finished my coffee, and Rajesh was just about ready to finish his own. This was less a condemnation on the staff than it was how terrible my nap on the plane was.
"I'll take the eggs royale and a croissant, thanks," I said in more of a rushed tone than I had meant.
"And I, the ultimate full English breakfast and, sure,  glass of the White Gold."
"Oh! Right," when Rajesh offered me a meal, I was not sure that drinks at six in the morning were included. "I'll have the same."
"Would you prefer a bottle, then?" asked the waitstaff.
"Sure, a bottle, then," Rajesh answered.
"Merci," the waitstaff said and walked off with our orders.
Rajesh shrugged, "It's happy hour somewhere in the world. So, Maddy, what are you doing around here, then?"
"I want to surprise some friends," I said instinctively, "I think. I don't know, this whole trip was rather... out of the blue. Found a week free and, well, here I am.
"What do you do otherwise, then? If you don't mind my asking, that is."
"I'm a creative consultant - I keep horns off the helmets of Vikings in movies, or wooden teeth from presidents in period dramas."
Beneath my casual tone, though, I felt the familiar itch of boredom---every "exciting" gig was just another checkbox on my résumé, never the thrill I craved.
I could tell that he was trying to decide whether or not the question on the tip of is tongue was one worth asking. He tilted his head more than a few times, and more than a few of them were accompanied by a jaw left slightly ajar, and a forefinger slightly aloft. Our waitstaff took this slight pause as an opportunity to deliver our meals and pour our wines.
Rajesh was a darker skinned gentleman, and even that being the case, the embarrassment was shining on his cheekbones.
"What do you do, then? Looks like it makes you enough money."
"A little bit of this, a little bit of that," Rajesh replied. I was not impressed and I figured I did not look it, either.
"Well, I used to work as a TA at the University of British Columbia, but was recruited for a much more... lucrative position. Of sorts."
"What kind of... sorts?" I asked.
Rajesh squinted his left eye in concentration, "I am a historical consultant, I travel around, checking out old sites and talking to people about this kind of thing; It's a bit like being a detective, following clues and trying to piece together a bigger picture."
"Not dissimilar to what I do, except that your job seems to be well funded, hah."
"Heh," he replied.

Rajesh and I sat together drinking our wine and more coffee refills than we had anticipated needing that early in the morning. I finished my meal with an apple tart, he finished his with a phone call, and delved even deeper into these sigils of his; each intricate line and curve seemed to draw her in further, my brow furrowing in concentration.
"You mind if I get this?" his expression shifting from relaxed to focused as he discussed something important. I watched as he gestured with his free hand, the other cradling his glass of wine.
As he wrapped up the call, he flashed me an apologetic smile, his cheeks slightly flushed from the wine and the conversation. I waved the pictures in his direction as he rushed off, but he paid them no mind. I nodded back and he left me with a few twenties.
With my courtesies now relieved of their duty, I pulled out my phone and checked my news feeds while finishing my risotto. While finishing another coffee I looked up where the Avis parked its cars, and how much time I had left to burn.

I looked up the B&B I had my reservation at, found which cab to take where, when, and for how much. It was about seven minutes away, but those were seven minutes in airport traffic that I thought best left to the professionals.

I take the last bite of my breakfast, feeling a little sad as I think about the strangely particular man I met on the plane. It was far from the most invigorating and in-depth conversation in the world, but finding someone worth talking to is not quite as easy as it was as a kid, or when our grades depended on us working with other people at uBir.
As I gather my things to leave, I notice something on the table next to me. It's a book, seemingly left behind by the Rajesh. I pick it up and examine it closely. It was a well-worn copy of whatever it is, but whatever it is, is not written on the cover, and those deckled edges are to die for.

## Introductions ##

As the car wound its way along towards Tintagel, a twinge of disappointment couldn't help but settle somewhere in my gut. I had invested so much time and effort into my education, pursuing my Master's with the hope of unlocking a world of opportunities. Yet here I was --- stuck working as a creative consultant for TV shows and films in Vancouver. + Every morning I'd get another email about trimming a Spartan's helmet plume or policing the neckline on Tudor gowns, and my heart would sink a little further. It felt like a far cry from the kind of work I went to school for.

Is this really all there is?

I pondered, a sigh escaping my lips. My role often felt more about keeping historical inaccuracies at bay than engaging with anything important While I took pride in my work, and I liked it fine, I longed for something more meaningful, something that resonated with the essence of history rather than just giving advice producers don't pay attention to.
I glanced out the window, watching the rugged coastline draw closer. The project at Tintagel gave me hope --- volunteer work, yes, but at least I was glancing at something that felt more important; more significant. driven by my desire to dive into something significant. I craved involvement in a project that felt important, something that would connect me to the rich tapestry of history I had studied for so long.
"Maybe this is my chance," I thought, my heart racing with a mix of anticipation and anxiety. I wanted to contribute to something tangible, to be a part of uncovering stories that had been buried for centuries. The inscriptions at Tintagel held the potential for discovery, and I was eager to explore that world.
I shook my head slightly, pushing aside the lingering doubts. "You've got this, Maddy," I reminded myself. "This is an opportunity to make a difference, to help illuminate the past." I hoped that by immersing myself in the work at Tintagel, I would find the fulfillment I had been searching for and perhaps redefine what my career could truly be.
The dig at Tintagel looked much like the dozens I'd seen before. On one side, graduates and undergraduates busily wielded their brushes and dustpans, eager to put their studies to use. On the other side were those getting paid--where I was headed. I was far too old to be paid in exposure; exposure didn't cover rent, especially in Vancouver.
Tintagel, the rocky promontory in Cornwall, had been in the news ever since the discovery of a 1300-year-old windowsill. But Eydís wasn't here for just any old windowsill; she was particularly interested in one inscribed with Latin, Greek letters, and Christian symbols.
Though I was too old to believe in legends like King Arthur and Merlin, I wouldn't have earned my MA in Medieval Studies if I wasn't at least fascinated by it all.

As I stepped out of the car, the salty sea breeze greeted me, carrying the unmistakable scent of the ocean. The Beach Cafe at the end of Castle Road bustled with tourists looking to visit the home of King Arthur before the summer ended. And despite the Americans; not a gun to be found.
After exchanging quick goodbyes to my ride, I made my way to the entrance of the cafe, where I grabbed a coffee, a Cornish pastry, and slipped a bottled lemonade in my Gran's bag.  I fished out my battered leather journal---Gran's old field notes she'd pressed into my hands---and scrawled a few thoughts on the crest of Tintagel Castle before zipping it back in. It was about time I got to work, I thought, as I buttoned up my coat.

With a final glance at the cafe, I turned and headed up the Southwest Coast Path. The trail wound along the rugged cliffs, offering views of the ocean below, that I had long-since tired of.
The path was well-worn, lined by wildflowers and tufts of grass swaying in the breeze. I focused on the rhythm of my footsteps, the crunch of gravel beneath my boots, and the distant sound of seagulls calling overhead. The landscape around me was very alive, and at the same time, very dead.
As I climbed higher, the remains of Tintagel Castle emerged in the distance, it's crumbled walls about as old as the Roman stones the path was made of, or the cliff faces I made sure to avoid bumping into. I quickened my pace, being more excited about having the chance to be good at something than my thinking there was something to actually find.

Finally, as I crested the hill, the dig site came into full view. The archaeologists were busy at work, their vests bright against the earth-toned surroundings. It felt good to be important --- even if you aren't. Even if you are a dime a dozen. Even if you know you were the last on the call sheet.
The late summer sun hung low in the sky, bathing everything in a warm glow, but the salty breeze carried a chill that sent a very tactile, very sticky chill. I spotted a small team of archaeologists gathered around a chunk of slate; their bright reflective vests stood out against the muted tones of the landscape, a splash of colour amidst the earthy browns and greys of the ruins.
I stepped towards thick webbing of green mesh fencing that marked the perimeter of the dig site when they noticed me

"Ah, there you are," one of the workers peeked outside of one of the trenches, their knees with leather patches sewn on; dirt and bright yellow stains in abundance.
He patted his hands on his pocket and reached one out: "Lee Hui, Site Manager. I believe I am the one who called you here."
"Madeleine C.M. Maycott," she said, shaking back with an awkward confidence, "you can call me Maddy."
He offered a polite nod, voice calm---yet I noticed his fingers tapping the side of his clipboard, as though each tap was urging the work to begin.
"I hired you to look at some symbols we found, and we can see where to go after that ," he began, gesturing towards the small folding desk of photos, laptops, weights, and coffee.
I joined them at the edge of the excavation area, where a careful grid had been laid out, marked by small stakes and string. I unzipped Gran's bag for the finger-less gloves she'd sewn into the lining and slid them on before crouching to examine the slate fragment. The team had dug down several feet, revealing layers of soil interspersed with stone, each layer telling a part of the castle's story.
"We've been focusing on this area right here," Lee explained, pointing to a section where the ground had been carefully excavated. "This is likely where part of the castle's wall stood, and we've uncovered some incredible artifacts." Lee gestured to a nearby table where various items were laid out---pieces of pottery, small tools, and fragments of slate. "But the real highlight has been the slate windowsill we found.
"We're trying to document everything meticulously," Lee continued. "This isn't just about digging up artifacts; it's about understanding the context in which they were used."
Though his words were measured, he couldn't resist shifting his weight back and forth---heel to toe---against the trench's edge, as if itching to carry on with the next step.

As I examined the slate windowsill, my fingers lightly traced the intricate inscriptions. I turned to Lee Hui, who I could tell was already thinking what I was thinking.
"Lee," I began, adopting a more formal tone. "These inscriptions reflect a far more complex interplay of languages and cultures than history has suggested so far."
I pointed to the Latin words fili and viri duo, "and the use of Latin here indicates that it was not merely a spoken language but likely part of formal instruction. Given the historical context, it's plausible that Arthur, and others of his status, received education in this very setting."
Next, I gestured towards the Greek letters and Christian symbols, "the inclusion of Greek suggests a broader intellectual engagement. It points to an educational environment that embraced multiple languages, which would have been essential for a leader in a multicultural context."

I knew that look on Lee's face---expectant, but not disappointed. He knew what he was talking about, as did the people he worked at that dig with. But for finds as significant as this one, any bit of confirmation was welcome.

I then highlighted the unique letter A intertwined with the V, "This symbol's potential connection to divinity further supports the idea that the teachings here were not just linguistic but also imbued with deeper philosophical and theological concepts. Again, such an education would have been crucial for a future king."
Lee's eyes lit up with understanding. "So, you're suggesting that this site was not just a royal base, but a centre for intellectual and linguistic development for Arthur?"
"Precisely," I confirmed. "Or an Arthur equivalent. If he lived here, he did not do so alone, or without a teacher... but...but there is something else."
"Sorry?" his workers had since given us space, so I was the only one to see him look confused.

Then, just at the edge of my vision, something flickered --- a hint of movement in the corner of my eye, and as my gaze wandered, the shape began to take form.
Slowly, the vague outlines coalesced into a two-dimensional figure. It became a five-pointed star---each point sharp and deliberate, cradled by a delicate arc of light. As I focused more intently, the shape began to fade, slipping away like a fleeting dream tied to a lingering feeling.
Instinctively, I reached out---my fingers hovering above the lines before finally touching the stone. The cool surface felt textured under my fingertips, each line telling a story that was both ancient and immediate. I traced the shape of the pentagram, feeling the subtle grooves and ridges, as if the very stone held the whispers of those who had come before.

"Can you feel that?" I murmured, glancing at Lee. "There's something almost tangible about it, like---."

The air thickened. My breath caught---and the world felt... wrong, like a page had turned before I finished reading.

# 1538 #

## Finchale Priory ##

### Welcome ###
--- I don't know what just happened, one minute I was... me. In a cave underground. Standing, breathing, grounded, then... I woke up.

Only I didn't.

I was awake, but not in the way that made sense. I was somewhere else, someone else. My thoughts were mine, but not all of them were. When I woke up, it was not me who had. I was awake, but I wasn't me who had woken. Her name was... Frances? Our name? It felt like both of our names; I felt that I was Frances, but I also knew that was Madeleine.

 Madeleine Catherina-Marie Maycott, to be precise.

We pulled ourselves to our feet --- but they didn't feel like mine. They didn't feel like my feet at all. My hands did not look like my own when they picked up the book beside us. When I swung my arms forward, they weren't mine, and when I stood up, I didn't stand as tall as I remembered. When I stepped forward, I didn't. When I didn't step forward, I did. I was still in control of my body, but none of it's movements felt like mine. I could look all about me, but nothing else did a lick of anything. My breath was steady, but the lungs were not mine.
It was like sleep paralysis, except my body kept moving. It just wasn't me moving it, and it wasn't really my body either. I could feel what she felt, I could feel that her feet had thinner ankles, callused doles, and did not have my preferred level of arch support.
My hands looked wrong. Narrower. Paler. Younger. When I flexed my fingers, they obeyed, but not the way I remember. Like the lag of a dream where your limbs forget their cues.

Her name was Frances. Frances Bennett.

As we stepped outside a bright red little number into the hot, morning sun, I saw the carriage were we on had worn gold wheels and an oak tree on the front door. Frances tapped at the wheel brake as she stepped outside, that book in one hand, and a handful of a wine red gown in the other. Frances was not used to walking around in dresses nice enough to have a fur lining --- I was not used to wearing one at all.
We parked a river that carved it's way past alder and birch trees, right outside a swaddling of small monastic buildings that also served as a small rest house for a group of Durham monks to our right --- and to our right we headed.

"What were you reading back there, anyway?" a voice asked.

John. His name was John.

His words reached us from far away, like sound filtered through cheesecloth, but as my consciousness regained itself, so did his identity.

He a cherry off its stem as he and his temporary protégé leisurely strode through the delicate decorated cloister, past an old man drinking tea and muttering to assorted rodentia.

"The Canterbury Tales, by Chaucer."
"Now that's a name I haven't heard in a while..." John uttered to himself as he handed over the carriage to be taken to the back, "did they not have that at Epke Abbey?"
"Not in a readable condition, we didn't. What do you mean you haven't heard of  Chaucer in a while?" Frances asked with an unexpected astonishment.
"We do not read such stories in university, Frances. Not when you are studying among the likes of  {==Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples==}{>>a French theologian and a leading figure in French humanism<<} and {==François Dubois==}{>>a French Huguenot painter. <<}..."
"Yeah, yeah, I get it, you're smart."
{=="And soon, my dear, you will be too---provided you can keep up. This work isn't exactly tailored for... convent readers."==}{>>He admits she is smart in the end<<}

After a few more of the leftover cherries, and a few more silent accolades from the visiting monks, John Leland and Frances Bennett were lead past the Frater and through the priory's south isle, the transept, and the quire. It was to be neither the first, nor the last monastery that she would spend time at, but it was most certainly one of the most important ones.

Top two, at least.

We settled into the chapter house that was overlooking the cloister garden. The ease with which Frances proceeded to the library gave hint to how long she had been doing this.
The library in the chapter house was welcoming, relaxing, and just cool enough to bear the summer heat as it crept towards midday. It was about twenty rows of shelves deep, between which lay a brick pathway leading under a wooden arch, a globe, and a very bright, very wide bay window. She ran her hand along the seam of the globe. Most people missed this part---the tiny warp in the equator, like a lid. Frances had a habit of finding such things
"Good morning," welcomed one of the volunteers.
"G'morning," said Frances.
"Ooh!" Frances whispered to herself, at pointing to the small wooden placards on either ends of the building, one was a white dragon, one was a red dragon, and both wore their Welsh inspiration with four legs instead of two.
"The two halves of the Pendragon crest," described one of the librarians, catching her awe of it, "Godric was a big fan of King Arthur,"
"I am among distinguished men, then," John replied. Frances was not quite sure what he meant by this, but I was.
And so, they started. Not at the front, not at the back, but at the first book Frances got a real good look at, because if she was going to spend the next few weeks reading books in a library, Frances thought it best to make at least part of it interesting.

Frances wasn't quite sure what religious order Finchale belonged to.  She did that John Leland worked for King Henry VIII, thought, and that was good enough if not for her, than for Mother Catherina. When she taught Frances to read and to write, she also taught her to, above all, know what to interpret, and when.
Kitty (for that is how she was best known to her students) always knew that Frances had an aptitude worth bringing to fruition. She hoped that travelling with Mr. Leland the king might help with that.
And Leland, for all his scholarly warmth, asked too many quiet questions about the monks. Not aloud---but to Frances, always to Frances, as if testing what she noticed when he wasn't looking.
Her inquisitive nature and bright mind were what persuaded Mr. Leland to give her a chance. Her intuitive nature and bright mind were much more than he had ever anticipated. She could look at the shape of a keyhole and sense which tumblers needed turning. It unnerved locksmiths. And thrilled her.

{==Epke Abbey==}{>>Based off of Bardney Abbey<<} was a Benedictine monastery founded in {==932==}{>>Oma’s birthday: September 18, 1932<<} by Herman Josef VII. Though it saw many leaders in its years standing, it remained small, quaint, personable, and offered of the few academic educations available to the 'fallen women' the medieval world. Young girls were sent to such institutions as often for education as to divert them from what were deemed vicious lives.
These women were called oblates; Frances was one of those oblates, and Catherina Bootsveld was one of those teachers.

Most of the libraries consisted of other works by Chaucer, transcriptions of plays like "The Summoning of Everyman", and the three parts of "The Ordinalia," but that isn't what they were here for. Not in Finchale. Finchale Priory, along with the classics of the age, also housed works deemed heretical, so were collected those deemed heretical, banned, and not yet burned. Works like the Liber Razielis Archangeli[^fn1] grimoire, Sic et Non by Peter Abelard, and the Manichaean Texts. If Mr. Leland were going to find anything of particular interest, it would be here.

She had wondered if Leland was truly there to study---or to sentence. The king wanted records, yes, but also leverage. Every forbidden book was a threat to his rule---or a tool, in the right hands.

Since his squire was a woman, John rest assured knowing that if Frances learned (and shared) anything untowards on her travels she, would be deemed too much a heretic to be taken seriously. Sometimes she learned about eunuchs, sometimes she learned that there was once a book of the bible called the Epistle of Barnabas.

Mother Bootsveld was not known to make mistakes. And Finchale Priory was not known for revealing its secrets.

### Stone buildings ###
After stepping down from the carriage, they passed through the priory gates. The church ahead was large and imposing, with a nave, transepts, choir, and presbytery.
The walls were decorated with carved stone capitals, tracery windows and painted frescoes. The floor was covered with tiles and gravestones. Frances paused to admire the double piscina and the sedilia built into the south wall---where priests once washed their hands and rested during mass.
She noticed a small chapel on the north side of the choir, dedicated to St John the Baptist. She recalled that this chapel had once been hermitage of St Godric, a former sailor and merchant turned hermit who had lived here as for fifty years before being buried beneath its floor. His life had been recorded by Reginald of Durham, one of the monks who had moved to Finchale after his death.
They crossed the cloister, passing other priory buildings. They saw the chapter house, where the monks met to discuss their affairs; the refectory, where they ate their meals in silence; the library, infirmary, and the guest house, where they welcomed visiting pilgrims.

They also saw the gardens, orchards, and fields surrounding the priory, where the monks grew their own food and herbs. It was a self-sustaining, harmonious community, guided by the rule of St Benedict.
They reached the gatehouse, where they were greeted by the porter, a friendly and talkative monk who asked them about their journey and their work. He pointed them towards their quarters, but also invited them to join the monks for supper and compline; the last service of the day.

The buildings at Finchale Priory were nestled in a green valley by the river Wear, encircled by woods and rolling fields. She felt a sense of peace and wonder as she walked around the grounds, admiring the architecture and the gardens.
She wandered towards the church, hoping to see a few monks inside. She entered through the arched doorway and was greeted by a sight that took her breath away. The church was filled with light and colour, from the stained glass windows that depicted scenes from the Bible and the lives of the saints.
The walls were decorated with paintings and frescoes, and the ceiling was vaulted and painted with stars. The altar was covered with a cloth embroidered with gold and silver threads, and behind it was a large crucifix that seemed to watch over the whole space.
She felt awe and reverence swell in  her chest as she moved slowly down the nave, drinking in the details of the art and architecture. She noticed that there were a few monks in the church, some praying in front of the side chapels, some reading from their books or rosaries. They wore simple brown robes with hoods, and had shaved heads or tonsures. Their expressions were serene,  yet shadowed by quiet resignation.
Frances wondered if they knew that their priory was doomed, and what they would do when they had to leave. She felt sorry for them, but also admired their faith and devotion. She wanted to talk to them, to learn more about their lives and beliefs, but she did not want to disturb them or offend them.
She chose to approach one monk who seemed friendlier than the rest. He was sitting on a bench near a window, holding a book in his hands. He had a round face with a gentle smile, and a long white beard that reached his chest. He looked elderly, but his eyes were bright --- alive with something youthful and curious.
Frances walked up to him and bowed slightly. "Excuse me, sir," she said politely. "May I speak with you for a moment?"
The monk looked up from his book and smiled warmly at her. He closed his book and set it aside. "Of course, my child," he said kindly. "What can I do for you?"
Frances felt relieved by his friendly tone. She introduced herself as Frances Bennet, squire to John Leland, who was surveying the library for King Henry VIII.

The monk nodded. "I know who you are," he said, a twinkle in his eye. "I've seen you with Master Leland in the library---a very learned man. And you, young Frances, are a brave soul indeed."
Frances blushed slightly at his compliment. "Thank you, sir," she said modestly. "But I am not brave at all. I am just doing my duty."
The monk chuckled softly. "Duty is a form of bravery," he said wisely. "And so is curiosity."
Frances smiled back at him. She liked this monk already. He seemed kind and wise, unlike some of the other monks who looked stern and cold.
She decided to ask him his name.
"I am Father Iroh," he said.
"Father Iroh," Frances repeated. "That is an unusual name."
"It is not my original name," Father Iroh explained. "It is a name I chose when I became a monk."
"Where are you from?" Frances asked.
"I am from China," Father Iroh said. "I left my homeland in search of truth," he murmured, "though sometimes I suspect what I found was my exile, not my pilgrimage."
"China?" Frances exclaimed in surprise. "That is very far away."
"Yes, it is," Father Iroh agreed. "But I have travelled a lot in my life."
"How did you come to England?" Frances asked.
"The question isn't how, but why," he said, a wistful smile flickering across his face. ""I was sent away in search of peace, but I arrived a stranger in every land I entered. Only here did I begin to feel like I belonged---but it's a long story," he added with a sigh. "But I will tell you if you have time to listen. "
"I have time," Frances said eagerly.
Father Iroh smiled again. "But first," he said, rising slowly, "you must eat."

### Dinner ###
The refectory was a large hall with wooden tables and benches, decorated with tapestries and paintings depicting scenes from the Bible. A large fireplace provided warmth and light, and a crucifix hung on the wall above it.
The dinner featured an array of breads, cheese, soup, vegetables, and fish. The food was simple but nourishing, and Frances and John Leland ate with gratitude and appreciation. They also drank watered-down wine from wooden cups, and listened to Father Iroh's stories and jokes. Father Iroh was a cheerful and wise man, who had a quiet passion for history---and for things left untold.

"What are you really hoping to accomplish here at Finchale, John?" Father Iroh asked, sipping at his cup of tea.
John Leland was taken aback by the question, and tried to act casual. He sipped his tea and smiled politely. "I was told you were informed, Father. I'm here to study the history and culture of this place, and to survey your libraries. I'm a scholar and a librarian, after all. That's what I do."
Father Iroh nodded, but his eyes were sharp and piercing. He knew that John Leland was more than a scholar and a librarian. The letter he had received a fortnight earlier had warned him: John Leland carried a royal commission--- authority to collect, assess, and confiscate any texts he deemed valuable... or dangerous.
John Leland's task was to look for and collect books and manuscripts from monasteries, libraries, and other places, and to write about the condition and history of the kingdom.

"The old monk is... cleverer than he lets on. Keep your eyes open, will you? I'd like to know what sort of stories he tells when I'm not around."

He had access to the king's library and archives, with the authority to confiscate any material that he deemed valuable or dangerous for the crown. Father Iroh knew this, but he wanted to see how he would react to questioning.

In the eyes of the King, a book could be a matchstick---or a lit fuse. Leland was the hand that judged which should be shelved and which should burn.

"Ah, of course," he said, with a light chuckle. "How could I forget?"
"I can give you---"
"---no, it's fine. I trust you," said Iroh with a smile that, to most at the table, would have seemed entirely sincere. Frances, however, was not most people.

Father Iroh also knew that Finchale Priory was not an ordinary monastery. It was said to be a sanctuary for seekers and scholars, protected by something older than stone or scripture. Some whispered that it could not be found by accident, nor remembered by those who came without purpose.
It did not, it seemed, always work.

Father Iroh decided to test John, and see if he could trust him. He leaned forward and looked at him intently. "Tell me, John---do you know why Finchale is so difficult to find? What makes it... different?"
John Leland felt a chill run down his spine as he met Father Iroh's gaze. He sensed that he was being scrutinized and challenged, and that his answer would have consequences. He tried to think of something plausible and harmless to say.
He cleared his throat and said: "I suppose it's because it's in a remote location, surrounded by woods and hills. And because it's an old and humble place, not very impressive or noticeable."

Father Iroh shook his head slowly. He could tell that John Leland was concealing something. He could also tell that he knew more than he let on.

Father Iroh leaned back, eyes half-lidded, his voice shifting into something slower, more deliberate---like a man reciting a story that's been told many times, but only to the right ears.
 "You know, it's said that Finchale Priory is protected by nature itself, a tale whispered among the villagers. They speak of how the woods and hills grow thick and dense, forming a barrier that shields the priory from those who might wish it harm. The paths twist and turn, confounding any who wander too close, leading them astray or back to where they started."
He glanced around, ensuring they were alone, and lowered his voice. "The sounds and sights of the priory are said to be faint, almost elusive, making it difficult for anyone to remember what they saw or heard. Only those with true purpose---those seeking knowledge, wisdom, or a connection to Godric---are believed to find their way through nature's defences."
Iroh spoke like a man who had been watching the world from the edge for too long---a man who had once been turned away, and had learned to make thresholds sacred---and who liked it there. Perhaps because he knew what it meant to be kept out, to wander too long among the lost. Pilgrimage teaches you what it means to never fully arrive.
Iroh paused, a knowing glimmer in his eyes. "Of course, as a man of the cloth, I cannot confirm such stories. But neither would I dare to deny them. After all, God works in mysterious ways, doesn't He? It's a story that holds meaning for many, and perhaps there's truth in it that even I must acknowledge."
Frances looked at him, torn. Leland would call this heresy. The Church would burn the very words Iroh spoke. And yet---her heart leaned toward the man who dared to wonder.
"Father Iroh, your words remind me of Pslams chapter 90, verse 2, where it says, 'He shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector, and my refuge: my God, in him will I trust[^fn2],' This suggests that nature itself, in all its majesty, is a reflection of God's protection and guidance. Perhaps it is through the very elements surrounding Finchale Priory that we find a divine safeguard."
"But of course," he said, as though it had always been obvious.

Iroh paused for a moment, then turned to his guests: "You are welcome here, both of you---but it is not my opinion that governs this place. And for your safety... tread with care."

After dinner, they retired to their rooms, thanked God for their day and seeking His guidance for tomorrow. They extinguished their candle and lay down in their cozy quarters with straw mattresses and wool blankets.

## Work - 1 ##

### Work ###
They got straight to work the following day. John said nothing, but Frances could see the warning from the night before had landed poorly. He was a man of the cloth---this Father Iroh. Sure, he was as welcome as any guest, but John couldn't understand how a monk could be so openly in touch with nature, and how he could ignore or defy the king's authority and doctrine. He couldn't help but think that Father Iroh was more druid than priest---more shaman than servant of the crown. A man called by something older than the Church.

Frances and John reached the chapter house, a stone building where the monks held meetings and kept their records. He knocked on the door, and heard Father Iroh's voice inviting him in. He opened the door, and saw Father Iroh and Frances sitting at a table covered with books and papers. They smiled at him and greeted him warmly. They asked him how he slept, and if he was ready for a day of work.
John Leland forced himself to smile back, and to act casual. He joined them at the table, and pretended to be interested in their findings. He tried to push his problem aside, and to focus on his task. He told himself that he was here to do his job as a scholar and a librarian, not to judge or condemn anyone.
Frances watched him with quiet curiosity, noting the stiffness in his posture, the slight narrowing of his eyes. He was loyal---she didn't doubt that. They both were.
To think the King's own agent had sent her here---her, an oblate from Epke. Surely it meant something.
Whatever they found here, it would serve a purpose. His purpose.

But John couldn't shake off his problem, or his doubts. He couldn't ignore his feelings, or his conscience. Later that evening, as they catalogued books side by side, John said lowly:
"I don't question his piety, mind you. Just... note anything odd he says. You've a better ear for that sort of thing."

The bay window in the eastern choir overlooked the Wear. Five slender lancet panes stood tall, divided by pale stone mullions and filled with stained glass scenes from Christ's life---and, unexpectedly, the old gods.
The central window shows the Crucifixion, when Jesus was nailed to a cross and died for the sins of humanity. The scene includes Mary and John at the foot of the cross, and two thieves on either side of Jesus. The background is purple, representing sorrow and royalty.
The second window from the left shows the Annunciation, when the angel Gabriel announced to Mary that she would conceive and bear a son. The angel holds a lily in his hand, a symbol of purity, and Mary holds a book, a symbol of wisdom. The background is blue, representing the sky and heaven.
The second window from the right shows the Nativity, when Mary gave birth to Jesus in a stable in Bethlehem. The scene includes Joseph, the ox and the ass, and a star shining above. The background is red, representing the earth and blood.
The leftmost window depicted the Crescent Moon---a silver disc with a face, framed by twin crescents and a scatter of stars. A symbol of the old goddesses, still lingering in sacred glass.

Leland was ecstatic. He felt like he had entered a treasure trove of knowledge and wisdom. He began to examine each book and manuscript carefully, noting down its title, author, date, contents and condition. He also looked for any annotations, marginalia or illustrations that might reveal more information or secrets. He was especially interested in anything that related to British history or legends, such as King Arthur, Merlin or Brutus; Anglo-Saxon ecclesiastical texts, manuscripts of historical and literary works, and relics and monuments.
Frances joined him quietly, hands already moving before words passed between them. She shared his enthusiasm for learning and discovery. She also had a keen eye for detail and beauty. She admired the craftsmanship and artistry of the books and manuscripts, especially those that were illuminated with gold and colours. She marvelled at the skill and devotion of the scribes and artists who had created these works.
They worked together for hours, oblivious to the passage of time. They felt like they were in another world, a world of books and manuscripts that spoke to them of the past and the present. With each book came a flicker of recognition---something only Frances seemed to feel. A warmth in the ink, a hum beneath the parchment. As if the pages remembered.

Mother Bootsveld was a wonderful woman, and while her scope was shallow, she at least knew this. She soon began to realize that the written word was not something to be feared or dismissed, but rather something to be celebrated and cherished. She saw in Frances a kindred spirit, someone who shared her love of learning and her passion for understanding the world around her.
While Mother Bootsveld knew that the world of literature was still beyond her grasp, she recognized the importance of nurturing and supporting those who showed promise in this field. She saw in Frances someone who could carry on the tradition of scholarship and learning, preserving and interpreting the knowledge of the past for future generations.

What she never imagined was how far into the future those generations might reach.

Frances paused before a shelf filled with ancient manuscripts, her breath catching in her throat. She carefully lifted one from its resting place, cradling it gently in her hands. The parchment was old and brittle, but the words inscribed upon it were still legible, written in a flowing script that was a soon to be long forgotten work of art itself.

They fell into a rhythm. Frances would retrieve a book, note its title and author. John would leaf through, scanning for marginalia, unfamiliar symbols, or anything... off. They worked quietly, but not without purpose.
The books in the chapter house were varied and fascinating. They ranged from ancient manuscripts written in Latin, Greek, or Hebrew, to modern books printed in English, French, or German. They covered topics such as theology, philosophy, history, geography, astronomy, medicine, alchemy, and magic. Some of them were rare and valuable, some of them were common and mundane. Some of them were familiar and recognizable, some of them were obscure and mysterious.
Setting aside his doubts about Father Iroh, John let his curiosity take over.. Not as a job, but as a passion. They were especially drawn to the ones they did not recognize, or that had no clear title or author. They would spend more time on these books, trying to decipher their contents and origins.
They would sometimes read aloud passages that caught their attention, or that puzzled or amused them. They would sometimes share their opinions or insights on what they read, or ask each other for help or clarification.

Father Iroh would come in and leave the chapter house with no apparent routine. He had other duties and responsibilities as the prior of the priory, and he also liked to wander around the grounds and commune with nature.
Sometimes, Iroh would appear with tea---no schedule, no fanfare, just there when the air felt heavy or the shadows too long. He would also join them in their conversation, and offer his wisdom and guidance. He would sometimes tell them stories or anecdotes about the books they surveyed, or about the history and culture of the priory. He would sometimes give them hints or clues about the Book of Wellspring, or about other secrets of the priory.

Frances and John appreciated Father Iroh's visits, and his generosity and kindness. John may have remained skeptical, but Frances respected Father Iroh deeply---his knowledge, his gentleness, and his quiet joy in the natural world.

He spoke like a man who had been watching the world from the edge for too long---and who liked it there.

She enjoyed his company and his humour, and his enthusiasm and optimism, and especially, the little pet squirrel he kept on him.

# 201X #

## Landing ##

### Airplane ###
I woke up with an oxygen mask dangling in front of my face and a whole plane full of very confused people.

"Oh, bloody hell," I heard from the seat beside me.
"Bloody hell indeed," I replied.
A portion of the planes cabin was now on their feet, wandering, and bumping about the aisles between us, and a small portion still had their oxygen masks on. There was nothing to really worry about, but the air of panic was undeniable.
"Miss," someone called from a few rows ahead, "there's nothing to worry about... it's just air pressure, I---"
Someone passed between us and blocked the rest of the sentence, but I could guess where it was going.
I can't blame her, really, flying is scary enough, and that isn't even considering the gigantic metal tube we are all stuck inside of. I took the opportunity the commotion afforded me to get to the washroom before anyone else was comfortable enough to form a line.
I did my business, washed my hands and splashed my face a few times in anemic attempt to catch my own thoughts. With as much noise and commotion as this turbulence had caused, it made holding my head on straight	 more of a feat than usual.

*pscht*
"---Please make sure your seat backs and tray tables are in their upright positions, your seatbelts are securely fastened, and all carry-on items are stowed either under the seat in front of you or in the overhead bins.---"
*pscht*

I hobbled back to my seat, hip-checking a few men in sweatpants along the way, and shoved my laptop and whatever books I had crammed into the seat-back pocket into my Gran's bag. Feeling a pang of nerves, I rummaged through its depths for Gran's emergency snack pouch---half a bag of dried mango---and popped a piece into my mouth. With one headphone hanging loose, I spent the next half hour trying to pin it in place---the leather folds leaving an embarrassingly stubborn imprint on my forehead.

### Birmingham ###
Welcome to Birmingham read the cartoon pirate, it's print stretched along one-too-many terminal. It was busy, but that was to be expected, but it was too early for any of us to feel much in a hurry; we were just in the mood to meander to and fro, and to and fro we meandered.

"Right, yes, of course," I uttered, shaking myself out of whatever fog was sitting in and waved my ticket at the Express Lane terminal.
I have an iffy relationship with airports (if you can even call it that), I visit them often enough that I cannot help but have an impression on a few of them. They each have their eccentricities, but each existed in a world of their own: half in, half out; half homely enough to fit the city, half uncomfortable enough to keep the homeless from making the foyers their home.
This didn't always work, but it's why every airport felt as bleached and grey as every other airport. Some had their distinctive qualities, like the apocalyptic paintings in Denver, the wooden totems at Vancouver, or the wave pool at Munich, but I'm positive those exist mostly to remind people they took the right transfer.
Whether you get a Durian McFlurry in Singapore, Camembert donuts in Germany, or the McPatatas in Mexico, you are still eating at a McDonald's.

I felt a tap on my shoulder.
"Pardon?" I asked, turning around to see it was the guy from the seat beside me, he had dark skin, a fresh haircut, and new shoes, and was also waiting for his luggage.
"Did they ever give us our breakfast?"
"Goddamnit, I don't think they did," I replied, then recognizing what that feeling in the bottom of my stomach was.
We continued to exist within each others periphery as we waited until our luggage came by. It was no less awkward than one would expect.
"Where you coming here from?"
"Toronto, yourself?" When you are waiting for your luggage, everything looks like your luggage.
"Same," he said, yawning a bit of a yawn and trying to get whatever his coffee mug had left in it.
His eyebrows perked up when a blue, 100 litre spinner bag came by; mine perked when a much smaller, hard case one did. He offered to grab mine, too, and I was too tired to bother saying no.
"You come here often?" He asked.
"Not especially," I answered, "not lately."
"Mind if I offer to get you breakfast? My bosses treat...," he scratched an itch on the side of his head, "don't like to eat alone. And we can bond over a shared traumatic experience."
"Yeah," I yawned, pushed my glasses up the ridge of my nose and yawned again. Of course I could afford breakfast, I could probably even get reimbursed by Lufthansa, too, but a free meal is a free meal, and I still had to figure out what the rest of my day was going to look like.
"Yeah, sure," I repeated, not entirely sure if my previous answer had made it past my yawn.

There are three types of people at the airport --- those that have to budget their airplane trips, those that do not, and those that spend their time in the secret VIP airport lounges that none of us were supposed to know about.. The former of the three do not use luggage with wheels, and the latter of the three do not have to bother.
Well, and the kind that still has a four hour drive to make down to the other end of England.

"Bottega?" he asked.
"Yeah, sure, sounds good," he lead me past a Duty Free, a watch store, and a WHSmith bookstore on the departure lounge map I had saved on my phone. I was sitting at a solid 87% battery life and I felt like the Queen of bloody England.
We found seats right away and ordered two coffees and two waters right away, so at least I knew this guy and I were on the same wavelength.
"You come here often, then?" I asked, using my finely tuned womanly skills to figure out if he comes here often, noticing the price of the DOC Brut.
"Enough for them to notice me," he answered, "but not enough to remember where." He laughed, I laughed back.
"So," I asked with half of my laugh still on my face, "what do I call you, other than Isle Seat, I mean."
He laughed again.
"I've been called Rajesh my entire life, so we can go with that. It's a name my parents brought here from {==Puducherry==}{>>Where M. Nights family is from<<}, a small city in India."
"Well, my name is Madeleine, but I've been called Maddy my entire life."
I whipped open my menu with one hand and portioned some cream and sugar to my coffee with the other. It felt nice to speak words that were more than 'yes' or 'no,' and at more a rate than an intermittent one.

By the time the waitstaff had arrived, I had already finished my coffee, and Rajesh was just about ready to finish his own. This was less a condemnation on the staff than it was how terrible my nap on the plane was.
"I'll take the eggs royale and a croissant, thanks," I said in more of a rushed tone than I had meant.
"And I, the ultimate full English breakfast and, sure,  glass of the White Gold."
"Oh! Right," when Rajesh offered me a meal, I was not sure that drinks at six in the morning were included. "I'll have the same."
"Would you prefer a bottle, then?" asked the waitstaff.
"Sure, a bottle, then," Rajesh answered.
"Merci," the waitstaff said and walked off with our orders.
Rajesh shrugged, "It's happy hour somewhere in the world. So, Maddy, what are you doing around here, then?"
"I want to surprise some friends," I said instinctively, "I think. I don't know, this whole trip was rather... out of the blue. Found a week free and, well, here I am.
"What do you do otherwise, then? If you don't mind my asking, that is."
"I'm a creative consultant - I keep horns off the helmets of Vikings in movies, or wooden teeth from presidents in period dramas."
Beneath my casual tone, though, I felt the familiar itch of boredom---every "exciting" gig was just another checkbox on my résumé, never the thrill I craved.
I could tell that he was trying to decide whether or not the question on the tip of is tongue was one worth asking. He tilted his head more than a few times, and more than a few of them were accompanied by a jaw left slightly ajar, and a forefinger slightly aloft. Our waitstaff took this slight pause as an opportunity to deliver our meals and pour our wines.
Rajesh was a darker skinned gentleman, and even that being the case, the embarrassment was shining on his cheekbones.
"What do you do, then? Looks like it makes you enough money."
"A little bit of this, a little bit of that," Rajesh replied. I was not impressed and I figured I did not look it, either.
"Well, I used to work as a TA at the University of British Columbia, but was recruited for a much more... lucrative position. Of sorts."
"What kind of... sorts?" I asked.
Rajesh squinted his left eye in concentration, "I am a historical consultant, I travel around, checking out old sites and talking to people about this kind of thing; It's a bit like being a detective, following clues and trying to piece together a bigger picture."
"Not dissimilar to what I do, except that your job seems to be well funded, hah."
"Heh," he replied.

Rajesh and I sat together drinking our wine and more coffee refills than we had anticipated needing that early in the morning. I finished my meal with an apple tart, he finished his with a phone call, and delved even deeper into these sigils of his; each intricate line and curve seemed to draw her in further, my brow furrowing in concentration.
"You mind if I get this?" his expression shifting from relaxed to focused as he discussed something important. I watched as he gestured with his free hand, the other cradling his glass of wine.
As he wrapped up the call, he flashed me an apologetic smile, his cheeks slightly flushed from the wine and the conversation. I waved the pictures in his direction as he rushed off, but he paid them no mind. I nodded back and he left me with a few twenties.
With my courtesies now relieved of their duty, I pulled out my phone and checked my news feeds while finishing my risotto. While finishing another coffee I looked up where the Avis parked its cars, and how much time I had left to burn.

I looked up the B&B I had my reservation at, found which cab to take where, when, and for how much. It was about seven minutes away, but those were seven minutes in airport traffic that I thought best left to the professionals.

I take the last bite of my breakfast, feeling a little sad as I think about the strangely particular man I met on the plane. It was far from the most invigorating and in-depth conversation in the world, but finding someone worth talking to is not quite as easy as it was as a kid, or when our grades depended on us working with other people at uBir.
As I gather my things to leave, I notice something on the table next to me. It's a book, seemingly left behind by the Rajesh. I pick it up and examine it closely. It was a well-worn copy of whatever it is, but whatever it is, is not written on the cover, and those deckled edges are to die for.

## Introductions ##

As the car wound its way along towards Tintagel, a twinge of disappointment couldn't help but settle somewhere in my gut. I had invested so much time and effort into my education, pursuing my Master's with the hope of unlocking a world of opportunities. Yet here I was --- stuck working as a creative consultant for TV shows and films in Vancouver. + Every morning I'd get another email about trimming a Spartan's helmet plume or policing the neckline on Tudor gowns, and my heart would sink a little further. It felt like a far cry from the kind of work I went to school for.

Is this really all there is?

I pondered, a sigh escaping my lips. My role often felt more about keeping historical inaccuracies at bay than engaging with anything important While I took pride in my work, and I liked it fine, I longed for something more meaningful, something that resonated with the essence of history rather than just giving advice producers don't pay attention to.
I glanced out the window, watching the rugged coastline draw closer. The project at Tintagel gave me hope --- volunteer work, yes, but at least I was glancing at something that felt more important; more significant. driven by my desire to dive into something significant. I craved involvement in a project that felt important, something that would connect me to the rich tapestry of history I had studied for so long.
"Maybe this is my chance," I thought, my heart racing with a mix of anticipation and anxiety. I wanted to contribute to something tangible, to be a part of uncovering stories that had been buried for centuries. The inscriptions at Tintagel held the potential for discovery, and I was eager to explore that world.
I shook my head slightly, pushing aside the lingering doubts. "You've got this, Maddy," I reminded myself. "This is an opportunity to make a difference, to help illuminate the past." I hoped that by immersing myself in the work at Tintagel, I would find the fulfillment I had been searching for and perhaps redefine what my career could truly be.
The dig at Tintagel looked much like the dozens I'd seen before. On one side, graduates and undergraduates busily wielded their brushes and dustpans, eager to put their studies to use. On the other side were those getting paid--where I was headed. I was far too old to be paid in exposure; exposure didn't cover rent, especially in Vancouver.
Tintagel, the rocky promontory in Cornwall, had been in the news ever since the discovery of a 1300-year-old windowsill. But Eydís wasn't here for just any old windowsill; she was particularly interested in one inscribed with Latin, Greek letters, and Christian symbols.
Though I was too old to believe in legends like King Arthur and Merlin, I wouldn't have earned my MA in Medieval Studies if I wasn't at least fascinated by it all.

As I stepped out of the car, the salty sea breeze greeted me, carrying the unmistakable scent of the ocean. The Beach Cafe at the end of Castle Road bustled with tourists looking to visit the home of King Arthur before the summer ended. And despite the Americans; not a gun to be found.
After exchanging quick goodbyes to my ride, I made my way to the entrance of the cafe, where I grabbed a coffee, a Cornish pastry, and slipped a bottled lemonade in my Gran's bag.  I fished out my battered leather journal---Gran's old field notes she'd pressed into my hands---and scrawled a few thoughts on the crest of Tintagel Castle before zipping it back in. It was about time I got to work, I thought, as I buttoned up my coat.

With a final glance at the cafe, I turned and headed up the Southwest Coast Path. The trail wound along the rugged cliffs, offering views of the ocean below, that I had long-since tired of.
The path was well-worn, lined by wildflowers and tufts of grass swaying in the breeze. I focused on the rhythm of my footsteps, the crunch of gravel beneath my boots, and the distant sound of seagulls calling overhead. The landscape around me was very alive, and at the same time, very dead.
As I climbed higher, the remains of Tintagel Castle emerged in the distance, it's crumbled walls about as old as the Roman stones the path was made of, or the cliff faces I made sure to avoid bumping into. I quickened my pace, being more excited about having the chance to be good at something than my thinking there was something to actually find.

Finally, as I crested the hill, the dig site came into full view. The archaeologists were busy at work, their vests bright against the earth-toned surroundings. It felt good to be important --- even if you aren't. Even if you are a dime a dozen. Even if you know you were the last on the call sheet.
The late summer sun hung low in the sky, bathing everything in a warm glow, but the salty breeze carried a chill that sent a very tactile, very sticky chill. I spotted a small team of archaeologists gathered around a chunk of slate; their bright reflective vests stood out against the muted tones of the landscape, a splash of colour amidst the earthy browns and greys of the ruins.
I stepped towards thick webbing of green mesh fencing that marked the perimeter of the dig site when they noticed me

"Ah, there you are," one of the workers peeked outside of one of the trenches, their knees with leather patches sewn on; dirt and bright yellow stains in abundance.
He patted his hands on his pocket and reached one out: "Lee Hui, Site Manager. I believe I am the one who called you here."
"Madeleine C.M. Maycott," she said, shaking back with an awkward confidence, "you can call me Maddy."
He offered a polite nod, voice calm---yet I noticed his fingers tapping the side of his clipboard, as though each tap was urging the work to begin.
"I hired you to look at some symbols we found, and we can see where to go after that ," he began, gesturing towards the small folding desk of photos, laptops, weights, and coffee.
I joined them at the edge of the excavation area, where a careful grid had been laid out, marked by small stakes and string. I unzipped Gran's bag for the finger-less gloves she'd sewn into the lining and slid them on before crouching to examine the slate fragment. The team had dug down several feet, revealing layers of soil interspersed with stone, each layer telling a part of the castle's story.
"We've been focusing on this area right here," Lee explained, pointing to a section where the ground had been carefully excavated. "This is likely where part of the castle's wall stood, and we've uncovered some incredible artifacts." Lee gestured to a nearby table where various items were laid out---pieces of pottery, small tools, and fragments of slate. "But the real highlight has been the slate windowsill we found.
"We're trying to document everything meticulously," Lee continued. "This isn't just about digging up artifacts; it's about understanding the context in which they were used."
Though his words were measured, he couldn't resist shifting his weight back and forth---heel to toe---against the trench's edge, as if itching to carry on with the next step.

As I examined the slate windowsill, my fingers lightly traced the intricate inscriptions. I turned to Lee Hui, who I could tell was already thinking what I was thinking.
"Lee," I began, adopting a more formal tone. "These inscriptions reflect a far more complex interplay of languages and cultures than history has suggested so far."
I pointed to the Latin words fili and viri duo, "and the use of Latin here indicates that it was not merely a spoken language but likely part of formal instruction. Given the historical context, it's plausible that Arthur, and others of his status, received education in this very setting."
Next, I gestured towards the Greek letters and Christian symbols, "the inclusion of Greek suggests a broader intellectual engagement. It points to an educational environment that embraced multiple languages, which would have been essential for a leader in a multicultural context."

I knew that look on Lee's face---expectant, but not disappointed. He knew what he was talking about, as did the people he worked at that dig with. But for finds as significant as this one, any bit of confirmation was welcome.

I then highlighted the unique letter A intertwined with the V, "This symbol's potential connection to divinity further supports the idea that the teachings here were not just linguistic but also imbued with deeper philosophical and theological concepts. Again, such an education would have been crucial for a future king."
Lee's eyes lit up with understanding. "So, you're suggesting that this site was not just a royal base, but a centre for intellectual and linguistic development for Arthur?"
"Precisely," I confirmed. "Or an Arthur equivalent. If he lived here, he did not do so alone, or without a teacher... but...but there is something else."
"Sorry?" his workers had since given us space, so I was the only one to see him look confused.

Then, just at the edge of my vision, something flickered --- a hint of movement in the corner of my eye, and as my gaze wandered, the shape began to take form.
Slowly, the vague outlines coalesced into a two-dimensional figure. It became a five-pointed star---each point sharp and deliberate, cradled by a delicate arc of light. As I focused more intently, the shape began to fade, slipping away like a fleeting dream tied to a lingering feeling.
Instinctively, I reached out---my fingers hovering above the lines before finally touching the stone. The cool surface felt textured under my fingertips, each line telling a story that was both ancient and immediate. I traced the shape of the pentagram, feeling the subtle grooves and ridges, as if the very stone held the whispers of those who had come before.

"Can you feel that?" I murmured, glancing at Lee. "There's something almost tangible about it, like---."

The air thickened. My breath caught---and the world felt... wrong, like a page had turned before I finished reading.

## Finchale Priory ##

### Welcome ###
--- I don't know what just happened, one minute I was... me. In a cave underground. Standing, breathing, grounded, then... I woke up.

Only I didn't.

I was awake, but not in the way that made sense. I was somewhere else, someone else. My thoughts were mine, but not all of them were. When I woke up, it was not me who had. I was awake, but I wasn't me who had woken. Her name was... Frances? Our name? It felt like both of our names; I felt that I was Frances, but I also knew that was Madeleine.

 Madeleine Catherina-Marie Maycott, to be precise.

We pulled ourselves to our feet --- but they didn't feel like mine. They didn't feel like my feet at all. My hands did not look like my own when they picked up the book beside us. When I swung my arms forward, they weren't mine, and when I stood up, I didn't stand as tall as I remembered. When I stepped forward, I didn't. When I didn't step forward, I did. I was still in control of my body, but none of it's movements felt like mine. I could look all about me, but nothing else did a lick of anything. My breath was steady, but the lungs were not mine.
It was like sleep paralysis, except my body kept moving. It just wasn't me moving it, and it wasn't really my body either. I could feel what she felt, I could feel that her feet had thinner ankles, callused doles, and did not have my preferred level of arch support.
My hands looked wrong. Narrower. Paler. Younger. When I flexed my fingers, they obeyed, but not the way I remember. Like the lag of a dream where your limbs forget their cues.

Her name was Frances. Frances Bennett.

As we stepped outside a bright red little number into the hot, morning sun, I saw the carriage were we on had worn gold wheels and an oak tree on the front door. Frances tapped at the wheel brake as she stepped outside, that book in one hand, and a handful of a wine red gown in the other. Frances was not used to walking around in dresses nice enough to have a fur lining --- I was not used to wearing one at all.
We parked a river that carved it's way past alder and birch trees, right outside a swaddling of small monastic buildings that also served as a small rest house for a group of Durham monks to our right --- and to our right we headed.

"What were you reading back there, anyway?" a voice asked.

John. His name was John.

His words reached us from far away, like sound filtered through cheesecloth, but as my consciousness regained itself, so did his identity.

He a cherry off its stem as he and his temporary protégé leisurely strode through the delicate decorated cloister, past an old man drinking tea and muttering to assorted rodentia.

"The Canterbury Tales, by Chaucer."

"We do not read such stories in university, Frances. Not when you are studying among the likes of  {==Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples==}{>>a French theologian and a leading figure in French humanism<<} and {==François Dubois==}{>>a French Huguenot painter. <<}..."

After a few more of the leftover cherries, and a few more silent accolades from the visiting monks, John Leland and Frances Bennett were lead past the Frater and through the priory's south isle, the transept, and the quire. Top two, at least.

We settled into the chapter house that was overlooking the cloister garden. The ease with which Frances proceeded to the library gave hint to how long she had been doing this.
The library in the chapter house was welcoming, relaxing, and just cool enough to bear the summer heat as it crept towards midday.
