## Mother Nature ##

### Stone buildings ###
After stepping down from the carriage, they passed through the priory gates. The church ahead was large and imposing, with a nave, transepts, choir, and presbytery.
The walls were decorated with carved stone capitals, tracery windows and painted frescoes. The floor was covered with tiles and gravestones. Frances paused to admire the double piscina and the sedilia built into the south wall---where priests once washed their hands and rested during mass.
She noticed a small chapel on the north side of the choir, dedicated to St John the Baptist. She recalled that this chapel had once been hermitage of St Godric, a former sailor and merchant turned hermit who had lived here as for fifty years before being buried beneath its floor. His life had been recorded by Reginald of Durham, one of the monks who had moved to Finchale after his death.
They crossed the cloister, passing other priory buildings. They saw the chapter house, where the monks met to discuss their affairs; the refectory, where they ate their meals in silence; the library, infirmary, and the guest house, where they welcomed visiting pilgrims.

They also saw the gardens, orchards, and fields surrounding the priory, where the monks grew their own food and herbs. It was a self-sustaining, harmonious community, guided by the rule of St Benedict.
They reached the gatehouse, where they were greeted by the porter, a friendly and talkative monk who asked them about their journey and their work. He pointed them towards their quarters, but also invited them to join the monks for supper and compline; the last service of the day.

The buildings at Finchale Priory were nestled in a green valley by the river Wear, encircled by woods and rolling fields. She felt a sense of peace and wonder as she walked around the grounds, admiring the architecture and the gardens.
She wandered towards the church, hoping to see a few monks inside. She entered through the arched doorway and was greeted by a sight that took her breath away. The church was filled with light and colour, from the stained glass windows that depicted scenes from the Bible and the lives of the saints.
The walls were decorated with paintings and frescoes, and the ceiling was vaulted and painted with stars. The altar was covered with a cloth embroidered with gold and silver threads, and behind it was a large crucifix that seemed to watch over the whole space.
She felt awe and reverence swell in  her chest as she moved slowly down the nave, drinking in the details of the art and architecture. She noticed that there were a few monks in the church, some praying in front of the side chapels, some reading from their books or rosaries. They wore simple brown robes with hoods, and had shaved heads or tonsures. Their expressions were serene,  yet shadowed by quiet resignation.
Frances wondered if they knew that their priory was doomed, and what they would do when they had to leave. She felt sorry for them, but also admired their faith and devotion. She wanted to talk to them, to learn more about their lives and beliefs, but she did not want to disturb them or offend them.
She chose to approach one monk who seemed friendlier than the rest. He was sitting on a bench near a window, holding a book in his hands. He had a round face with a gentle smile, and a long white beard that reached his chest. He looked elderly, but his eyes were bright --- alive with something youthful and curious.
Frances walked up to him and bowed slightly. "Excuse me, sir," she said politely. "May I speak with you for a moment?"
The monk looked up from his book and smiled warmly at her. He closed his book and set it aside. "Of course, my child," he said kindly. "What can I do for you?"
Frances felt relieved by his friendly tone. She introduced herself as Frances Bennet, squire to John Leland, who was surveying the library for King Henry VIII.

The monk nodded. "I know who you are," he said, a twinkle in his eye. "I've seen you with Master Leland in the library---a very learned man. And you, young Frances, are a brave soul indeed."
Frances blushed slightly at his compliment. "Thank you, sir," she said modestly. "But I am not brave at all. I am just doing my duty."
The monk chuckled softly. "Duty is a form of bravery," he said wisely. "And so is curiosity."
Frances smiled back at him. She liked this monk already. He seemed kind and wise, unlike some of the other monks who looked stern and cold.
She decided to ask him his name.
"I am Father Iroh," he said.
"Father Iroh," Frances repeated. "That is an unusual name."
"It is not my original name," Father Iroh explained. "It is a name I chose when I became a monk."
"Where are you from?" Frances asked.
"I am from China," Father Iroh said. "I left my homeland in search of truth," he murmured, "though sometimes I suspect what I found was my exile, not my pilgrimage."
"China?" Frances exclaimed in surprise. "That is very far away."
"Yes, it is," Father Iroh agreed. "But I have travelled a lot in my life."
"How did you come to England?" Frances asked.
"The question isn't how, but why," he said, a wistful smile flickering across his face. ""I was sent away in search of peace, but I arrived a stranger in every land I entered. Only here did I begin to feel like I belonged---but it's a long story," he added with a sigh. "But I will tell you if you have time to listen. "
"I have time," Frances said eagerly.
Father Iroh smiled again. "But first," he said, rising slowly, "you must eat."

### Dinner ###
The refectory was a large hall with wooden tables and benches, decorated with tapestries and paintings depicting scenes from the Bible. A large fireplace provided warmth and light, and a crucifix hung on the wall above it.
The dinner featured an array of breads, cheese, soup, vegetables, and fish. The food was simple but nourishing, and Frances and John Leland ate with gratitude and appreciation. They also drank watered-down wine from wooden cups, and listened to Father Iroh's stories and jokes. Father Iroh was a cheerful and wise man, who had a quiet passion for history---and for things left untold.

"What are you really hoping to accomplish here at Finchale, John?" Father Iroh asked, sipping at his cup of tea.
John Leland was taken aback by the question, and tried to act casual. He sipped his tea and smiled politely. "I was told you were informed, Father. I'm here to study the history and culture of this place, and to survey your libraries. I'm a scholar and a librarian, after all. That's what I do."
Father Iroh nodded, but his eyes were sharp and piercing. He knew that John Leland was more than a scholar and a librarian. The letter he had received a fortnight earlier had warned him: John Leland carried a royal commission--- authority to collect, assess, and confiscate any texts he deemed valuable... or dangerous.
John Leland's task was to look for and collect books and manuscripts from monasteries, libraries, and other places, and to write about the condition and history of the kingdom.

"The old monk is... cleverer than he lets on. Keep your eyes open, will you? I'd like to know what sort of stories he tells when I'm not around."

He had access to the king's library and archives, with the authority to confiscate any material that he deemed valuable or dangerous for the crown. Father Iroh knew this, but he wanted to see how he would react to questioning.

In the eyes of the King, a book could be a matchstick---or a lit fuse. Leland was the hand that judged which should be shelved and which should burn.

"Ah, of course," he said, with a light chuckle. "How could I forget?"
"I can give you---"
"---no, it's fine. I trust you," said Iroh with a smile that, to most at the table, would have seemed entirely sincere. Frances, however, was not most people.

Father Iroh also knew that Finchale Priory was not an ordinary monastery. It was said to be a sanctuary for seekers and scholars, protected by something older than stone or scripture. Some whispered that it could not be found by accident, nor remembered by those who came without purpose.
It did not, it seemed, always work.

Father Iroh decided to test John, and see if he could trust him. He leaned forward and looked at him intently. "Tell me, John---do you know why Finchale is so difficult to find? What makes it... different?"
John Leland felt a chill run down his spine as he met Father Iroh's gaze. He sensed that he was being scrutinized and challenged, and that his answer would have consequences. He tried to think of something plausible and harmless to say.
He cleared his throat and said: "I suppose it's because it's in a remote location, surrounded by woods and hills. And because it's an old and humble place, not very impressive or noticeable."

Father Iroh shook his head slowly. He could tell that John Leland was concealing something. He could also tell that he knew more than he let on.

Father Iroh leaned back, eyes half-lidded, his voice shifting into something slower, more deliberate---like a man reciting a story that's been told many times, but only to the right ears.
 "You know, it's said that Finchale Priory is protected by nature itself, a tale whispered among the villagers. They speak of how the woods and hills grow thick and dense, forming a barrier that shields the priory from those who might wish it harm. The paths twist and turn, confounding any who wander too close, leading them astray or back to where they started."
He glanced around, ensuring they were alone, and lowered his voice. "The sounds and sights of the priory are said to be faint, almost elusive, making it difficult for anyone to remember what they saw or heard. Only those with true purpose---those seeking knowledge, wisdom, or a connection to Godric---are believed to find their way through nature's defences."
Iroh spoke like a man who had been watching the world from the edge for too long---a man who had once been turned away, and had learned to make thresholds sacred---and who liked it there. Perhaps because he knew what it meant to be kept out, to wander too long among the lost. Pilgrimage teaches you what it means to never fully arrive.
Iroh paused, a knowing glimmer in his eyes. "Of course, as a man of the cloth, I cannot confirm such stories. But neither would I dare to deny them. After all, God works in mysterious ways, doesn't He? It's a story that holds meaning for many, and perhaps there's truth in it that even I must acknowledge."
Frances looked at him, torn. Leland would call this heresy. The Church would burn the very words Iroh spoke. And yet---her heart leaned toward the man who dared to wonder.
"Father Iroh, your words remind me of Pslams chapter 90, verse 2, where it says, 'He shall say to the Lord: Thou art my protector, and my refuge: my God, in him will I trust[^fn2],' This suggests that nature itself, in all its majesty, is a reflection of God's protection and guidance. Perhaps it is through the very elements surrounding Finchale Priory that we find a divine safeguard."
"But of course," he said, as though it had always been obvious.

Iroh paused for a moment, then turned to his guests: "You are welcome here, both of you---but it is not my opinion that governs this place. And for your safety... tread with care."

After dinner, they retired to their rooms, thanked God for their day and seeking His guidance for tomorrow. They extinguished their candle and lay down in their cozy quarters with straw mattresses and wool blankets.

### Work ###
They got straight to work the following day. John said nothing, but Frances could see the warning from the night before had landed poorly. He was a man of the cloth---this Father Iroh. Sure, he was as welcome as any guest, but John couldn't understand how a monk could be so openly in touch with nature, and how he could ignore or defy the king's authority and doctrine. He couldn't help but think that Father Iroh was more druid than priest---more shaman than servant of the crown. A man called by something older than the Church.

Frances and John reached the chapter house, a stone building where the monks held meetings and kept their records. He knocked on the door, and heard Father Iroh's voice inviting him in. He opened the door, and saw Father Iroh and Frances sitting at a table covered with books and papers. They smiled at him and greeted him warmly. They asked him how he slept, and if he was ready for a day of work.
John Leland forced himself to smile back, and to act casual. He joined them at the table, and pretended to be interested in their findings. He tried to push his problem aside, and to focus on his task. He told himself that he was here to do his job as a scholar and a librarian, not to judge or condemn anyone.
Frances watched him with quiet curiosity, noting the stiffness in his posture, the slight narrowing of his eyes. He was loyal---she didn't doubt that. They both were.
To think the King's own agent had sent her here---her, an oblate from Epke. Surely it meant something.
Whatever they found here, it would serve a purpose. His purpose.

But John couldn't shake off his problem, or his doubts. He couldn't ignore his feelings, or his conscience. Later that evening, as they catalogued books side by side, John said lowly:
"I don't question his piety, mind you. Just... note anything odd he says. You've a better ear for that sort of thing."

The bay window in the eastern choir overlooked the Wear. Five slender lancet panes stood tall, divided by pale stone mullions and filled with stained glass scenes from Christ's life---and, unexpectedly, the old gods.
The central window shows the Crucifixion, when Jesus was nailed to a cross and died for the sins of humanity. The scene includes Mary and John at the foot of the cross, and two thieves on either side of Jesus. The background is purple, representing sorrow and royalty.

The second window from the right shows the Nativity, when Mary gave birth to Jesus in a stable in Bethlehem. The scene includes Joseph, the ox and the ass, and a star shining above. The background is red, representing the earth and blood.

Leland was ecstatic. He felt like he had entered a treasure trove of knowledge and wisdom. He began to examine each book and manuscript carefully, noting down its title, author, date, contents and condition. He also looked for any annotations, marginalia or illustrations that might reveal more information or secrets. He was especially interested in anything that related to British history or legends, such as King Arthur, Merlin or Brutus; Anglo-Saxon ecclesiastical texts, manuscripts of historical and literary works, and relics and monuments.
Frances joined him quietly, hands already moving before words passed between them. She shared his enthusiasm for learning and discovery. She also had a keen eye for detail and beauty. She admired the craftsmanship and artistry of the books and manuscripts, especially those that were illuminated with gold and colours. She marvelled at the skill and devotion of the scribes and artists who had created these works.
They worked together for hours, oblivious to the passage of time. They felt like they were in another world, a world of books and manuscripts that spoke to them of the past and the present. With each book came a flicker of recognition---something only Frances seemed to feel. A warmth in the ink, a hum beneath the parchment. As if the pages remembered.

Mother Bootsveld was a wonderful woman, and while her scope was shallow, she at least knew this. She soon began to realize that the written word was not something to be feared or dismissed, but rather something to be celebrated and cherished. She saw in Frances a kindred spirit, someone who shared her love of learning and her passion for understanding the world around her.
While Mother Bootsveld knew that the world of literature was still beyond her grasp, she recognized the importance of nurturing and supporting those who showed promise in this field. She saw in Frances someone who could carry on the tradition of scholarship and learning, preserving and interpreting the knowledge of the past for future generations.

What she never imagined was how far into the future those generations might reach.

Frances paused before a shelf filled with ancient manuscripts, her breath catching in her throat. She carefully lifted one from its resting place, cradling it gently in her hands. The parchment was old and brittle, but the words inscribed upon it were still legible, written in a flowing script that was a soon to be long forgotten work of art itself.

They fell into a rhythm. Frances would retrieve a book, note its title and author. John would leaf through, scanning for marginalia, unfamiliar symbols, or anything... off. They worked quietly, but not without purpose.
The books in the chapter house were varied and fascinating. They ranged from ancient manuscripts written in Latin, Greek, or Hebrew, to modern books printed in English, French, or German. They covered topics such as theology, philosophy, history, geography, astronomy, medicine, alchemy, and magic. Some of them were rare and valuable, some of them were common and mundane. Some of them were familiar and recognizable, some of them were obscure and mysterious.
Setting aside his doubts about Father Iroh, John let his curiosity take over.. Not as a job, but as a passion. They were especially drawn to the ones they did not recognize, or that had no clear title or author. They would spend more time on these books, trying to decipher their contents and origins.
They would sometimes read aloud passages that caught their attention, or that puzzled or amused them. They would sometimes share their opinions or insights on what they read, or ask each other for help or clarification.

Father Iroh would come in and leave the chapter house with no apparent routine. He had other duties and responsibilities as the prior of the priory, and he also liked to wander around the grounds and commune with nature.
Sometimes, Iroh would appear with tea---no schedule, no fanfare, just there when the air felt heavy or the shadows too long. He would also join them in their conversation, and offer his wisdom and guidance. He would sometimes tell them stories or anecdotes about the books they surveyed, or about the history and culture of the priory. He would sometimes give them hints or clues about the Book of Wellspring, or about other secrets of the priory.

Frances and John appreciated Father Iroh's visits, and his generosity and kindness. John may have remained skeptical, but Frances respected Father Iroh deeply---his knowledge, his gentleness, and his quiet joy in the natural world.

He spoke like a man who had been watching the world from the edge for too long---and who liked it there.

She enjoyed his company and his humour, and his enthusiasm and optimism, and especially, the little pet squirrel he kept on him.
